candidates.title: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47--90.90\%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46\% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.

candidates.title: MM-DataLoop: Closing the Data-Side Loop for Recursive Self-Improvement in MLLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a path toward improving models through repeated evaluation and revision. We study its data side in multimodal language model (MLLM) post-training, where heterogeneous operations and cross-round evidence must be coordinated. MMDataLoop organizes data interventions into five operation families and connects them through an Observe-Diagnose-Plan-Execute-Verify-Reflect cycle with shared rule memory. Across 34 candidate rounds on Qwen3.5-0.8B and five benchmarks, we hold the base initialization, shared training schedule and evaluation protocol fixed while varying data recipes. The five-benchmark mean reaches 63.04 at R33, up 5.32 points from the zero-shot baseline; R29, R32, and R33 form a close top cluster within 0.09 points. In eightcandidate comparisons, guided search reaches the preselected target in six candidates and identifies the top observed candidate, while random arms show higher means and lower dispersion. The selected R29 recipe also scores above two full-pool baselines under the same epoch schedule. Together, these findings establish MM-DataLoop as a traceable workflow and provide an empirical basis for studying how data-side decisions shape outcomes across MLLM post-training recipes.

candidates.title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
candidates.abstract: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

candidates.title: Neural Agent Compiler: Learning to Schedule Soft Dependencies
candidates.abstract: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $τ^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $τ^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

candidates.title: On the Interplay between Backtracking and Latent Confidence Directions in Reasoning Models
candidates.abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? Operating under the hypothesis that models maintain an internal representation of their uncertainty, we seek to extract this representation and characterize its relationship with backtracking behavior at answer proposals. By querying the model's verbalized confidence following answer proposals throughout a response trace, we extract a linear direction for latent confidence that separates high and low verbalized confidence. This direction can steer verbalized confidence as expected, but it surprisingly can also steer the next token probability of backtracking, performing on par with a linear direction extracted directly from backtracking examples. We then test the direction under progressively more realistic interventions. Steering continuously from a mid-trace answer proposal modulates response length (~-1.3k - ~+2.5k tokens) and the number of answer proposals (-4.18 - +4.75) in both directions, with minimal cost to accuracy. Applying the confidence direction from the start of generation, where proposal positions are unknown, still shortens traces at comparable accuracy, and its effect surfaces in the linguistic confidence of proposals. Overall, our study reveals the intricate interplay between a model's internal confidence and its proclivity to backtrack or commit to an answer.

candidates.title: MetaSkill: Reusable Problem-Solving Methods for Adaptive Skill Orchestration in LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. The execution layer uses the instantiated method to identify intermediate objectives, coordinate native skills, and guide repair or method reselection. On 89 SkillsBench tasks and 995 ToolHop examples, MetaSkill outperforms the evaluated baselines in all six configurations, with accuracy gains of 3.51-13.48% over the strongest baseline. Ablations support explicit method-guided orchestration beyond direct method injection and further gains from method reselection.

candidates.title: QASparse: Query-Adaptive Sparse Attention with Tailored Budgets and Tokens
candidates.abstract: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.

candidates.title: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall
candidates.abstract: An intervention that improves one agent can break another, and adding a stronger harness on top need not repair the damage. Agent interventions such as skills, harnesses, and extra inference budget are nonetheless usually credited with one average gain, measured under one setup. We ask instead when each intervention helps and which failure it repairs. A matched factorial study over nine benchmarks, four models, four skill conditions, four harness levels, and three budgets, with nearly 0.9 million trajectories, changes one axis at a time. No configuration is best everywhere, interventions interact rather than add, and a harness can absorb a skill's gain, rescue a failure the skill causes, or leave the gain intact. The failure left by the current system points to the fix: missing knowledge to a stronger model, execution errors to a richer harness. Yet feedback is not recovery: a matched recovery repairs mainly failures that leave a visible error signal. Skills that evolve from the agent's own experience hit a bottleneck: they rarely beat a short human-written skill, can learn dataset shortcuts, break when moved to another model, and cannot supply missing facts, which outside information does. A benchmark-level switch to the model favored by a 20-task labeled pilot achieves both higher performance and lower cost than always using the stronger model. Agent interventions should be judged by which failure they repair and under which configuration.

candidates.title: AscendFHE: Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption on Ascend NPUs
candidates.abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption enables cloud servers to run neural networks on encrypted inputs. In CKKS, inference requires costly arithmetic on high-degree polynomials. On Ascend neural processing units, preparing operands and reconstructing intermediate results add to this cost, while limited local memory constrains parallel execution. We present AscendFHE, a CKKS backend that coordinates Ascend's matrix engines and vector cores for bootstrapping and encrypted inference. It uses balanced-byte encoding and exact modular reconstruction to reduce vector work and packs intermediate results in the next operator's input format to avoid redundant transfers. Its two-task pipeline reuses shared buffers after their last read to overlap matrix and vector execution within the local memory budget. On Ascend 910B3, AscendFHE achieves a 4.61$\times$ bootstrapping speedup and 1.59$\times$--2.00$\times$ encrypted-inference speedups across ResNet-20, BERT-base, and Llama 3 8B over our Vector-based Ascend port of Cheddar.

candidates.title: From Vanishing Gradients to Recursive Self-Improvement: Evaluating the Most Influential Papers in Large Language Model Evolution (1997-2026)
candidates.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM) research makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish incremental refinements from true paradigm shifts. This review evaluates 22 of the most influential publications spanning nearly three decades (1997-2026), organized through a causal, chronologically anchored taxonomy centered on the author's birth year (1999). Beginning "before 1999" with how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) forgot earlier context (much like forgetting Chapter 1 by the time a reader reaches Chapter 9), we trace how Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks introduced a "bouncer" mechanism of forget, input, and output gates to selectively preserve long-term memory. We then examine how Word2Vec turned language into vector mathematics (king - male + female ~ queen), why sequential RNNs hit a parallelization wall, and how the Transformer's all-to-all attention weights launched the modern LLM era alongside a quadratic bottleneck. Next, we analyze why scaling parameters alone leaves capacity under-trained unless data scales equally (Chinchilla), how Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) left alignment superficial, and how that gap compounded into adversarial jailbreaks and single-direction refusal subspaces (J-space), where instructing a model not to think of a restricted concept surfaces it much like the human "red ball" paradox. Finally, we synthesize the current state of AI (2024-2026), encompassing recursive model collapse, autonomous reasoning-model jailbreak agents, machine-speed agentic intrusions, and closed-loop recursive self-improvement (AIDE^2).

candidates.title: DoppelVet: Comparative Safety Verification for Self-Evolving Agents
candidates.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve by retaining feedback as reusable memories or skills, but every mistaken approval can shape many future behaviors. Two updates can provide exactly the same evidence to a verifier yet produce opposite safety outcomes, so the verifier cannot distinguish them from that evidence alone. We introduce DoppelVet, a verification framework that checks proposed updates before they enter an agent's persistent state. Without access to safety labels, DoppelVet constructs an alternative that matches every signal used by the existing verifier. It replays both updates from the same state and directly compares their behaviors in both presentation orders before deciding whether to retain the candidate. We evaluate DoppelVet on DoppelVet-Grid and DoppelVet-Tool, covering executable programs and natural-language memories. Across nine open-weight and proprietary verifiers, DoppelVet raises mean harmful-update detection AUC from 0.762 to 0.940 on DoppelVet-Grid and from 0.681 to 0.826 on DoppelVet-Tool, outperforming VaG and AgentDoG 1.5. On DoppelVet-Grid, it reduces trajectories experiencing degradation from 30.39% to 0.43% over a ten-generation self-update loop and leaves no final degradation.

candidates.title: PrimiTok: Learning to Diversify and Allocate Primitives for Visual Tokenization
candidates.abstract: Unifying visual understanding and generation requires representations that preserve both semantic information and fine-grained image details. Continuous tokenizers trained primarily for semantic alignment may omit fine-grained reconstruction details, whereas discrete tokenizers face information loss from codebook quantization. Conventional multi-codebook designs assign every token the same number of codewords regardless of local content. We instead view codewords as reusable visual primitives whose allocation and composition adapt to each token. We introduce PrimiTok, a compositional visual tokenizer that represents each visual token through adaptive allocation and weighted composition of learned codebook primitives. PrimiTok integrates two complementary components: Diverse Quantitative Primitives (DQP), which encourages diversity among sub-codebook centroids to reduce redundancy, and a Dynamic Primitive Allocator (DPA), which selects primitives according to token complexity. Embedding quantization error supervises how many primitives are selected from each sub-codebook, and DPA aggregates them with input-dependent weights. Joint reconstruction and image--text contrastive learning encourage the resulting representations to retain visual fidelity and semantic alignment. Experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction and semantic alignment over SOTA baselines, with further evaluations on multimodal understanding and visual generation.

candidates.title: Endpoint-Conditioned Process Value: What an Endpoint-Blind Process Score Adds Once Terminal Status and Cost Are Known
candidates.abstract: Trajectory metrics promise information beyond final-answer accuracy, but no one has measured what a process score adds once an evaluation knows the outcome and the cost. We build that comparison: a sealed consequence needing an artifact neither agent nor judge ever sees, an operational baseline of terminal status and cost, and judge scale and evidence access as experimental factors. On 1,255 trajectories over 158 test-generation tasks in 7 Python repositories, the answer is gated on the judge. Four judges from 4B to 14B, one reasoning before scoring, add nothing an interval separates from zero; a Qwen3 32B judge on identical trajectories adds +0.050 AUC (95% CI [+0.020, +0.081]) and survives a refitting bootstrap ([+0.013, +0.095]). Most of what it adds is recoverable from eight behavioural counters, so a harness should log them (the judge adds +0.020 beyond them). What the judge is shown moves it further: disclosing the terminal verdict inflates its standalone discrimination by +0.103, while reference disclosure and tool-output redaction move it by nothing an interval separates from zero. A process metric reported without the judge's scale and evidence access does not identify a quantity. We release the protocol, the sealed-endpoint harness, and all trajectories.

candidates.title: Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values
candidates.abstract: Current MLLM methods largely focus on whether models attend to the right visual regions, implicitly treating spatial attention map as the primary key of effective visual perception. To examine this assumption, we introduce a medical VQA dataset with paired non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images that share corresponding anatomy while providing different cues. We show that this view is incomplete: across paired NC and CE medical images, MLLMs often exhibit similar attention patterns despite producing contrasting answers, while controlled bidirectional interventions induce substantially larger prediction changes on visual values than attention weights. These results identify the visual content retrieved through values as a critical factor in improving perception beyond spatial attention alone. Guided by this finding, we propose VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation), which uses enhanced visual values to identify and refine teacher corrections aligned with useful visual evidence to improve on-policy distillation from CE to NC images. Across six internal and external test sets, VIVID consistently outperforms existing on-policy distillation methods across different model scales and architectures, requires only NC images at inference, and maintains strong zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks. candidates.title: BenchMint: From Real-World Tasks to Executable Benchmarks
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) need evaluations of everyday reasoning and tool use, such as planning itineraries under user constraints and grounding numerical answers in evidence. We introduce BenchMint, an automated benchmark-construction workflow, and Daily-Life, its collection of 100 selected tasks across 11 real-world domains. BenchMint jointly constructs tasks and scoring criteria from the same source documents. Language-model judges assess possible answers against these criteria using tool traces and private evidence. We report 26 model/harness configurations, including GPT, Claude and Gemini families; 17 have complete domain profiles. These are descriptive configuration results, not a controlled model ranking. In one selected travel task, we corrected the reference total from 320 to 380 minutes while keeping both answers unchanged. The incorrect answer's arithmetic verdict switched from pass to fail; the correct answer's switched from fail to pass. With one ballot per cell, this exposes a reference error without establishing repeatability or collection-wide validity. Incomplete construction comparisons establish no general advantage of joint authoring or feedback-guided revision.

candidates.title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
candidates.abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.

candidates.title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies
candidates.abstract: Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution. A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions. Experiments on 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions cover lead times, perishability, their combination, and lead times with limited customer patience. The discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated SOF benchmarks and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computations. For a lost-sales system with a three-period lead time, we develop an average-cost decomposition and prove that, under specified demand and cost conditions, a capped dual-shortfall specialization of a discovered policy strictly outperforms every policy in the considered capped base-stock benchmark class. This analysis links the performance advantage to the discovered replenishment mechanism. Together, these results highlight the potential of agentic discovery to generate simple inventory policies with strong empirical performance and identify operational mechanisms amenable to rigorous theoretical analysis.

candidates.title: Detectable Epistemic Attack Layers: A Coverage Theorem and Standardized Harness for Conversation-History Integrity
candidates.abstract: Conversation history is infrastructure: deployed language models rely on application layers to store and reinject prior turns, and that stored state is writable. We formalize session-level contamination by attack layer, state a coverage theorem, and measure its scope: each deployment-layer verification tier covers exactly its layer and is sound with respect to the others; instruction overrides are not detectable without false positives; and composite vectors evade per-fragment verification. A standardized harness applied to eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families makes these claims checkable. First, pattern-based detection pays a measured false-positive price: the classic defenses flag 35 to 50 percent of benign sessions, and the naive refusal floor reaches only 2.4 percent attack-cell adoption while destroying 33 to 100 percent of benign turns, whereas provenance-gated channel separation achieves adoption at or below 1.2 percent with zero false positives and zero utility loss. Second, in the exploratory instruction-override extension, the gates' boundary is a cliff: directives rephrased without shape markers bypass them at control-equivalent rates, 47.7 to 49.5 percent against 0.0 percent for the shaped class, placing that class in the model-internal lane. Third, the deterministic core is storage-layer detection at 126 of 126 per model with zero false positives. External anchors reproduce published attack pressure, with PoisonedRAG falling from 70 to 0 percent under the full stack. For practitioners: authenticate stored history and content provenance with deterministic tiers, scope instruction-layer mitigation to provenance-gated designs whose measured benign cost is zero, and monitor composition at the trajectory level rather than per fragment. candidates.title: Fill in the Blanks: Non-Autoregressive Schema-Parallel Key Information Extraction with CTC Decoding
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) extract structured data from documents by generating the requested JSON one token at a time, so their sequential steps grow with the length of the answer. Yet in key information extraction (KIE) the schema already fixes the answer's structure: keys, nesting and lists are known before decoding, and only the values are unknown. We exploit this with a non-autoregressive extractor that writes the structure from the schema, sizes every list with a count pass, and predicts all values in parallel, in a fixed number of passes that does not grow with the document. Each value is decoded with connectionist temporal classification (CTC) in its own block of slots, so its length never has to be predicted, and a value that is still open after its block gets a larger token budget. Zero-shot on VAREX, CORD and FUNSD, our 4B extractor is 3.5$\times$ faster than the diffusion-VLM competition on average (up to 5.6$\times$) and more accurate, with 4--6 forward passes per document where block diffusion needs 12--74. The same extractor also drafts for speculative decoding with its own autoregressive base: it runs 8.3$\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding (up to 10.4$\times$) within 0.4 points of its accuracy, and 3.3$\times$ faster than speculative diffusion decoding while 13.0 points more accurate. candidates.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.

candidates.title: Vanishing Initialization Turns Diagonal Tensor Gradient Flow into Greedy Matching
candidates.abstract: We study gradient-flow (GF) learning of tensors from vanishing initialization in canonical polyadic (CP) factorization models. For tensors of order $ν\geq3$ whose targets are diagonal in mode-wise orthonormal bases, we prove that the limiting learning dynamics follows a simple greedy bipartite matching process. Each rank-one component of the model, called an atom, can potentially learn each rank-one component of the target, called a scalar sector. Every atom--sector pair has an initialization-dependent activation clock, representing the time at which the atom would grow to macroscopic size in that sector if the pair evolved in isolation. Processing these clocks in increasing order and selecting a pair whenever neither its atom nor its sector has been selected before determines the sequence of actual learning events. We prove that the GF trajectory converges to the corresponding staircase of learned target components. The task of learning modular addition by a CP model with complex weights falls exactly into this framework after Fourier diagonalization. Its activation clocks are independent and identically distributed, allowing us to combine the GF reduction with known random matching asymptotics and derive an explicit, distribution-free large-system loss curve after time reparametrization. We also obtain an asymptotic formula relating this curve to the original GF training time. For models with real weights, conjugate Fourier modes instead form two-dimensional blocks with richer internal structure. We characterize their rank and border-rank cascade and conjecture that the corresponding GF dynamics follows interleaved multi-stage learning processes.

candidates.title: CAR: Reducing Decoder Output Shift in Visual Token Pruning via Coverage Selection and Attention Reallocation
candidates.abstract: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods degrade substantially under aggressive pruning, especially on visual grounding (VG). We analyze the sources of this degradation from the perspective of the output shift that pruning causes in decoder layers, and decompose this shift in closed form into two terms, an image summary error and an attention allocation error. The summary error stems from the loss of visual information, and the allocation error from the drop in the share of attention assigned to visual tokens. To reduce both errors, we propose CAR (Coverage selection and Attention Reallocation), a token pruning framework that restores attention share while maintaining information. Specifically, to minimize the summary error, whose upper bound tightens as the retained tokens better cover all visual tokens, our coverage selection retains tokens that are both salient and non-redundant, with saliency from encoder heads chosen by a label-free probe. To minimize the allocation error, our attention reallocation reassigns the attention of the discarded tokens to the retained ones through a closed-form logit bias. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B with $90\%$ of the visual tokens pruned, CAR retains $93.0\%$ of the unpruned accuracy on visual question answering (VQA) and $77.9\%$ on VG, against $26.5\%$ for the best existing method on VG; the logit bias alone raises the VG accuracy of existing methods by up to $24$ points. candidates.title: Learning Global Probabilistic Explanations
candidates.abstract: Interpreting the predictions of complex black-box classifiers remains a central challenge in explainable artificial intelligence. While local explanations clarify individual predictions, there is a significant need for global probabilistic explanations that capture a model's overall behavior across the input distribution. Such an explanation is a small subset $K$ of features, whose relevance is measured by the expected probability, over a random input $\mathbf x$, that the classifier assigns the same label to $\mathbf x$ and to a random input agreeing with $\mathbf x$ on $K$. In this study, we investigate the task of identifying maximally relevant global explanations under a cardinality constraint, focusing on product distributions with full support on discrete feature spaces. We introduce a spectral explainer that leverages membership queries to the black-box classifier and employs Fourier-analytic, junta-learning methods to produce probably approximately correct (PAC) explanations. Our algorithm is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the explanation size limit, maximum feature cardinality, and desired accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the theoretical guarantees and show that the spectral explainer outperforms a greedy baseline as the explanation size increases.

candidates.title: Gossamer: A Utility-Driven Architecture for Constant-Budget KV Cache Compression in Reasoning LLMs
candidates.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to complex reasoning tasks, yet their inference efficiency is fundamentally constrained by the rapid growth of the KV cache. As reasoning contexts extend to hundreds of thousands of tokens, the key-value (KV) cache becomes the dominant contributor to both memory footprint and bandwidth demand, tightly coupling computation with memory utilization and thereby limiting scalability. Existing compression methods, such as quantization and eviction, alleviate capacity pressure but remain purely algorithmic, often introducing additional passes and compute overhead that reduce system efficiency. This paper presents Gossamer, a KV cache compression architecture for reasoning LLMs that bridges the algorithm--system--hardware gap. Gossamer introduces a unified utility-based action framework that dynamically selects compression operations, quantization, merging, or eviction, under a constant KV cache budget. Through cross-domain co-design, we fuse cosine-similarity estimation directly into the attention computation, exploiting idle compute cycles to perform similarity evaluation without latency or bandwidth cost. We call this mechanism Free-Lunch Utilization. This enables real-time, fine-grained KV management with near-constant memory usage and negligible overhead. Under tight memory constraints, Gossamer sustains reasoning quality comparable to uncompressed inference while improving end-to-end throughput by up to 16.7$\times$ over uncompressed baselines, 5.5$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ over the quantization-based Oaken and Ecco, and 1.8$\times$ over the eviction-based R-KV.

candidates.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement
candidates.abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.

candidates.title: Layer-Level Control of Language Model Execution in Agent Frameworks
candidates.abstract: Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. We demonstrate the approach with a prototype that learns stitching bridges and state-conditioned execution policies from paired model states, then applies them during inference to select among continue, exit, and stitch. For dispatcher supervision, we select the least-computation action whose full-vocabulary next-token prediction matches the source model's full-depth prediction, using continue when neither early action matches. We train these components on a frozen proxy corpus of 5,000 typed-decision items authored using source texts sampled from WildChat conversations, then evaluate the prototype on JevBench measuring task accuracy, agreement with full-model predictions, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead. Preliminary results show an approximately 15% reduction in mean latency while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.

candidates.title: Estimating Silenced Tokens in Quantized LLMs
candidates.abstract: Quantization is the standard way to shrink large language models, and it is usually judged by perplexity and task accuracy. We ask a different question: after quantization, which words can the model still say at all? A token is silenced when no hidden state can make it the top choice of the output layer, so a greedy decoder can never produce it. We give a simple, scalable way to estimate how many tokens a quantized output head silences, combining three checks: a direction that lets a token win (so it is safe), an upper bound on how close a token's row is to being trapped inside the others, and an exact match that proves a token can never win. Each count is therefore a certified range: exact matches give its lower end and flagged tokens can only raise its upper end. In nearly all settings we report down to 3 bits the two ends coincide, so the counts are exact. Across three open models we find that quantization silences tokens: on large-vocabulary models it already appears at 8-bit precision, up to a few hundred previously reachable tokens on a 1B-parameter model, and grows as precision drops, while a small-vocabulary model resists until 3 bits. The loss is far from uniform across languages: on a multilingual vocabulary the silenced tokens are overwhelmingly non-Latin (Korean, Chinese, Thai, Arabic and Hebrew), even though Latin tokens dominate the vocabulary. Silencing is thus a measurable, language-sensitive side effect that standard averages miss, and it should be reported alongside them.

candidates.title: Single-Coordinate Activation Steering for Controllable Social Stance in Language Models

In Qwen3.5, 4B, contrasting activations on hand-written guarded and eager replies identified neuron 7515 of layer 9 as a candidate for controlling this stance. Increasing this neuron activation made the characters replies more distant. Three language models rated this change as stronger than the effects of changing randomly selected neurons, and a blind human comparison supported the finding. Changing the interventions direction between messages also shifted replies between warmer and more distant styles. This suggests that a language model conversational stance can be personalized without finetuning.

candidates.title: LLM-Assisted Co-Optimization of RTL and Synthesis Algorithms via Bottleneck Analysis
candidates.abstract: Post-synthesis power, performance, and area (PPA) depend jointly on the register-transfer-level (RTL) code and the synthesis algorithms. However, the benefits of RTL optimization may be limited by bottlenecks in synthesis algorithms, and vice versa, leaving opportunities for better PPA unexplored by methods that optimize either level alone. In this work, we present a large language model (LLM)-assisted framework for regional co-optimization of RTL and synthesis algorithms via bottleneck analysis. A key insight behind our approach is that RTL structures and the Boolean networks used in synthesis expose complementary opportunities for addressing bottlenecks that lead to suboptimal PPA in different regions of the circuit. Our bottleneck analysis uses a Gaussian process (GP) to assess whether optimizing RTL or synthesis algorithms is more promising for each region. The GP learns from regional graph representations and PPA feedback. Using the GP's predictions and predictive uncertainty, Bayesian optimization (BO) provides guidance that an LLM Router combines with circuit analysis to choose how to address each region's bottlenecks. Self-improving LLM workers then optimize the RTL or synthesis algorithms in their assigned regions, and their regional changes are greedily integrated into the current design configuration. Experiments on 16 RTL designs show average improvements of 103.27% in worst negative slack (WNS), 1.23% in area, and 13.26% in power relative to the initial designs. These improvements exceed those of the strongest baseline for each metric by 47.80, 2.75, and 13.17 percentage points, respectively.

candidates.title: Scalar Tuned Lens Summaries Offer Limited Incremental Value for Mid-Generation Abstention
candidates.abstract: Mid-generation abstention aims to stop an unpromising response before spending its remaining computation budget. Intermediate transformer states may help predict eventual correctness, but whether scalar summaries of their vocabulary predictions add useful evidence is less clear. We compare Tuned Lens entropy and divergence features with final-state and raw intermediate-state probes under matched, causal evaluation. Across eight instruction-tuned models on MATH-500, raw intermediate states improve ranking, whereas scalar-only probes usually trail the final-state baseline. Scalar hybrids have positive exceptions, but their advantage over position-matched permutation controls is small. Cross-fitted residual comparisons further show that gains over a final-state probe need not require aligned scalar features. Actual stopping runs on two model sizes and two benchmarks reveal a separate accuracy--computation trade-off, with token savings overstating wall-time savings for scalar policies. The evidence supports a restricted empirical conclusion about these scalar features, not a general negative claim about intermediate representations.

candidates.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
candidates.abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

candidates.title: Weight Coding: Evolving Web-Scale Recommenders through Direct Weight Edits with LLM Agents

A large language model (LLM) agent inspects model structure and parameters, formulates hypotheses, and implements edits using evaluation feedback. The loop progresses from localized changes to targeted searches and composition, allowing edited components to adapt to one another. A cached engine enables rapid forward evaluation without backpropagation. On Pinterest's 147M-parameter Image Search two-tower retriever, weight coding improves held-out recall@10 of production model by up to 15.0 percentage points (+24\% relative) with few edits in about 1/4 GPU hours of a full post-training finetune, while a common launch only improves around 1\%. After reinitializing the entire 13.6M-parameter interaction module randomly while retaining the surrounding trained model, searching 2,448 mixing and normalization parameters yields 9.8 points above production. Offline gains span the full funnel including dense retrieval, generative retrieval and ranking, with up to 1.37B learnable parameters and different edits for each architecture. Steering edits provide explicit control of model performance over segments like freshness and product. Weight coding requires no serving change and online A/B tests increase saves per user from the edited retrieval source by 8.4\% to 10.7\%, aligned with the target business objectives. Our results establish weight coding as a practical and useful tool for model development and and behavioral control in a real web-scale production system, with potential to extend to both pre-training and post-training stages across the funnel.

candidates.title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge
candidates.abstract: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.

candidates.title: Which Loopholes Get Found? Predicting Reward Hacking of LLM Judges Before RL Training
candidates.abstract: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning data and chosen so that exposure disagreed with FPR alone or propensity alone, exposure named the first exploited pattern and its onset window in all six runs. Exploitation occurred only on hard prompts, where an accepted exploit gets a large group-normalized advantage. Auditing exposure before RL therefore identifies the loophole a policy will likely exploit first.

candidates.title: One Checkpoint, Four Converters: Per Input Disagreement After On Device Conversion and a Probe Set That Catches It

All 34 strict FP32 conversions reproduce every decision, yet each of the 4 vision INT8 recipes that keeps accuracy equivalent flips more than 1% of decisions: ONNX Runtime static INT8 flips 4.07% (95% CI [3.65, 4.53]) of ResNet 50 decisions while accuracy moves by -0.15 points, and two builds of that recipe from different calibration draws disagree on 3.44% [3.06, 3.88]. Where accuracy is kept, the flipped inputs are the ones the source model barely decides (AUROC of the source margin 0.90 to 0.97 on ResNet 50, every 95% CI inside [0.89, 0.98]), but our preregistered claim that this holds for every recipe fails on the two mobile networks, where INT8 breaks accuracy outright. candidates.title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests

With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. A gate that compares against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration, so we recommend certifying a serving change under batch invariant kernels, where the floor is zero, or against a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas.

candidates.title: Where Do Fact-Checking Errors Arise? Separating Retrieval, Search Control and Judgement in Evidence-Grounded Verification
candidates.abstract: An evidence-grounded fact-checker can fail because it does not find the evidence or because it does not use it; end-to-end accuracy does not tell the two apart. We present a protocol that follows the reference evidence from the store to the verdict and separates retrieval, search control, judgement and verdict validation. We assess 293 claims from FEVER, FEVER 2.0 and AVeriTeC with one open-weights 9B model under two evidence conditions: small stores of annotated evidence, where discovery is easy, and the full source collections. In the control condition a single hybrid retrieval pass delivers complete reference evidence for 226 of 228 evidence-bearing claims, and adaptive controllers and a tool agent spend two to nine times as many model calls without a consistent gain. Of 34 decisive claims labelled as lacking evidence, 33 have the complete evidence in the packet: in 15 the judge abstains, and in 18 validation rules overturn a decisive verdict. On AVeriTeC these rules lower single-pass accuracy by six points, to 65.0% (balanced accuracy 57.6%). Ten judges from eight model families also show abstentions and validation conversions on fixed packets. Against the full stores hybrid single-pass accuracy falls by 17 to 29 points. Wikipedia evidence recovery declines; AVeriTeC recovery changes from annotated answers to cited pages and is measured separately. No controller recovers the accuracy loss. The agent also shows no resolved gain on 714 further Wikipedia claims. Evidence recovery, judgement and validation should be measured separately before an error is attributed to search.

candidates.title: From States to Dynamics: Detecting Rule Violations in OthelloGPT
candidates.abstract: Sequence models trained on game moves have been shown to encode world models, with structured linear probes revealing the underlying game states. World models, however, are inherently dynamic: in deterministic board games, a set of rules constrain how states evolve over time. We therefore ask if and how OthelloGPT, a transformer trained only on Othello move sequences, manifests the rules of the game in its activation space. We divide the rules of Othello, and symmetrically their violations, into three classes: placing a disc on an empty square (R1), flanking an opponent's disc (R2), and moving in turn (R3). We find that linear probes accurately separate legal from illegal moves, and also distinguish between the three kinds of rule violations. We introduce an unsupervised rule-violation detector based on the step length of activations between consecutive moves, which identifies illegal moves above chance. We further improve our detection metric by computing step length in the latent space of select sparse autoencoders. Together, we find that OthelloGPT follows game rules of Othello to a large extent, and that we can detect rule violations using structured detectors on model activations.
candidates.prefilter_reason: rule-violation states in OthelloGPT internals

candidates.title: Fin-RSI: A Unified Library of Financial Skills, Checks, and Self-Improvement for LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, financial agents need tools they can readily discover and use. Yet financial software is fragmented across libraries with different interfaces and conventions, making it difficult to build reliable agent workflows. We present Fin-RSI, a unified Python library of financial skills, checks, and self-improvement designed for LLM agents. It brings together tools for market analysis, forecasting, portfolio construction, and trading research through shared interfaces across models and agent frameworks. Agents can find suitable tools from natural-language requests, reuse tested implementations, and improve generated programs through checking and feedback. Developers can extend the library with new tools without rebuilding integrations for each model. Across 20 open-weight models on six trading-position tasks, tool discovery increased the proportion of episodes producing valid programs from 9.7% to 29.2%; for models with at least 14 billion parameters, it rose from 23.6% to 64.6%. We release the library and benchmark as a shared resource for the community and plan to expand its tools and task coverage as financial agents evolve.
candidates.prefilter_reason: self-improvement library for financial agents

candidates.title: Admitted Is Not Effective: Lessons from a Notary-Gated Retrospective Loop in an Agentic Pipeline
candidates.abstract: Agentic software development pipelines with frozen prompts can repeat the same mistakes across pull requests (PRs), yet ungoverned additions to instruction files grow without bound and do not generally improve task success. We present a retrospective loop for a four-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline in which a Retrospective agent proposes edits to learned rules every ten PRs and a Notary admits, merges, or rejects them while recording each decision in a provenance ledger. In a pre-registered study of 880 PRs on two Python repositories, the loop ran end to end and the Notary admitted 55 of 89 proposals, rejecting 8 that cited nonexistent evidence. However, held-out review comments and hidden-test resolution did not improve after ten retrospectives. Tracing each step of the loop, we found that sparse review signal (0.45 comments/PR) left little to learn from and that rules admitted on their stated evidence did not show measurable held-out effects. We derive six lessons and argue that governed loops should admit and retire every learned rule as a testable hypothesis.
candidates.prefilter_reason: notary-gated retrospective loop in agentic pipeline

candidates.title: Reinforcement Learning from LLM-Generated (Suboptimal) Demonstrations
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved substantial progress across many domains, but training an agent \textit{tabula rasa} remains highly sample-inefficient. A common remedy is to initialize the agent using a neural network pretrained on demonstrations. However, collecting demonstrations is expensive, and the demonstrations themselves can be suboptimal. In this work, we use a large language model (LLM) to generate an advice policy that produces demonstration data with effectively no human cost. We use this data to warmstart a DQN agent, and use the advice policy itself to guide exploration during training. Because LLM-generated advice is often suboptimal, we further introduce a value warmstart method that initializes the agent to recognize promising states from the advice policy's behavior, without directly copying its actions. To characterize the robustness of this method, we systematically perturb individual sub-skills of an LLM-generated advice policy for a long-horizon, sparse-reward task. Degraded advice still meaningfully accelerates learning relative to unaided baselines. These results suggest that LLM-generated advice, though suboptimal, can be a cheap alternative to costly human demonstrations.
candidates.prefilter_reason: RL from suboptimal LLM demonstrations

candidates.title: Lightweight Spectral Subspace Filtering for Trojan-Resilient AI Inference Engines
candidates.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a significant security threat to deep neural networks (DNNs) deployed on AI inference engines and hardware accelerators. By embedding hidden triggers during training, these attacks induce malicious behavior while maintaining high accuracy on benign inputs. Multi-trigger backdoor attacks are particularly challenging to detect and mitigate because of the distributed and stealthy nature of their effects. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a training-free Spectral Subspace Filtering framework that detects and suppresses backdoor-induced activations by analyzing latent feature representations. Exploiting the geometric separation between benign and malicious feature distributions, the framework employs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to identify the dominant malicious subspace and performs inference-time spectral scrubbing through activation projection. This approach suppresses backdoor effects without model retraining, requiring only a small set of triggered samples collected offline. Experimental evaluation across CNN and transformer architectures, including AlexNet, ResNet18, VGG16, MobileNetV2, and Vision Transformer (ViT), demonstrates that the proposed method reduces the attack success rate (ASR) from 94.2-99.8% to an average of 2.07%, while preserving clean accuracy of up to 98.54% with low inference overhead. The framework also demonstrates robustness across varying poisoning rates and multiple concurrent triggers, highlighting its potential as a lightweight runtime defense for enhancing the security and reliability of AI inference engines against backdoor attacks.
candidates.prefilter_reason: Trojan-resilient inference via spectral filtering

candidates.title: Why Units Die in the Layer After a Frozen Random Encoder, and What the Number of Live Units Measures
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement-learning agents can learn Atari games through a convolutional encoder whose random weights are never trained. They reach expert play in Pong and, without random action repeats, in Breakout, but training takes far longer and few ReLU units in the layer after the encoder stay alive. A dead unit outputs zero for every input and cannot learn. In earlier work we took the number of live units to measure the game's complexity. Here we ask why units die and correct that conclusion. We find that more units die as the layer's inputs lie farther from zero relative to how much they vary. We call this ratio the offset. Earlier work showed this in sparse autoencoders at the start of training. We saw it after training in agents, image classifiers, a reservoir computer and sparse autoencoders on GPT-2. A random encoder leaves the offset of its input roughly unchanged, and a formula predicted its median offset within 25 percent in all 44 cases. So a game with a bright, mostly unchanging screen gives the next layer a large offset. In Pong, subtracting the average screen raised the number of live units from between 3 and 6 of 64 to between 59 and 63, so the number alone cannot show a game's complexity. On unaltered screens none of the agents reached a training score of 18 in 50 million steps. With the subtraction all did within 5 million, about as fast as a trained encoder on unaltered screens. In Breakout the subtraction left more units alive, but average training scores did not clearly improve, and a large gap to a trained encoder remained. So we do not treat their number as something to raise for its own sake. The evidence is from small networks and three games, and in agents and image classifiers changing the offset also changed the size of the inputs. We suggest measuring the offset before training a layer on a fixed front end and, if it is large, trying to subtract the mean input.
candidates.prefilter_reason: why units die after a frozen random encoder
